doc.title: Terry Gibbs interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 5, 2021 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Idols Eldridge and Young, and technique without direction on vibes
summary: Gibbs says he admired Roy Eldridge and Lester Young, had technique but no idea what to do with it, disliked held vibraphone notes, and describes a pedal invention for vibrato.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: In fact, twenty plus years ago you said, about that period in your life when Dizzy and Charlie Parker were coming up with this new thing, you said, “I almost had a nervous breakdown. I stumbled on Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie and it was something so new to me I was looking for in my life, because I had all this technique and I didn’t know what to do with it.”

That’s true. But actually my idols — I never had idols, the people I really admired were Roy Eldridge and Lester Young. And you know how they played, they played beautiful notes, they played pretty, but never a lot of notes. And I had all this technique and I didn’t know what to do with the technique. I mean you know, and especially in those days when Milt Jackson used to — the motor would come out where he would slow down the motor or adjusted it to what vibrato you want. Even that I didn’t like — I liked it because I liked the slow motor but the point is I couldn’t land on a note and maybe feel that emotion of a vibrato, like a trumpet player can go [scats]. So hitting that note and holding it wasn’t what I wanted to hear. So I had to get off of it. I had to get off like well you see Dizzy and Bird, they can hold a note because it’s a saxophone. And they liked the sound they got out of it. And so they can hold a note with me — I only held a note, there were times where it was the emotion I felt with the vibrato, you know?

You know one time Monk, I was working on an invention where you know you have pedals, where you hold, you press down and hold a note to sustain the note. I had double pedals where you can press the other one at the same time and it would adjust the motor — it would go judging to where maybe you want to hear it. You know you would learn, just like a tympani player when the two tympanis came in, because I was an old tympani player. I used to have to do it with the handles. Today they just, with their foot, they press down and they get to the note they want. You know? That’s what I wanted with the vibrato. I was going to get to where I could press down and it would get to the vibrato that I wanted to hear and I’d stop. You know there’d be numbers so you’d know exactly, you’d learn what number vibrato, you know there’d be different ones which I, with my brain, have the idea but not the brain how to put it together. I always had ideas but never knew what to do with them.
